subtype: Approach: holding a structured decision meeting [Action]
passage: Kunal sent the brief at nine on Monday: one page, three options for the vendor portal, with costs and risks under each. By Wednesday's meeting in the fourth-floor room in Pune, printouts lay at every seat. He told the group each team would get five minutes, no interruptions, and set a timer on his phone. Arnab from finance spoke first about the cost of the second option; the engineers followed on risk; sales asked for a date. When the timer rang, people stopped, sometimes mid-sentence. Kunal wrote the decision on the whiteboard, option two with a phased start, and under it the three reasons people had raised. He mailed the same notes within the hour. A few still wished for another result, but Arnab said, 'At least we all got heard.'

qa.q: How many minutes did each team get to speak?
What might Arnab have felt when saying 'At least we all got heard'?
qa.a: Arnab probably felt respected and somewhat settled, even without full agreement, because the process gave every group a turn.

qa.q: What other approach could Kunal try if two groups still disagree after the meeting?
qa.a: Kunal could ask each side what it truly needs and look for a middle option, since a phased start already shows that compromise can meet several concerns.

qa.q: How might the engineers see the timer?
qa.a: The engineers may find it fair because they got the same time as sales, though they might also feel five minutes is short for explaining risk.

grounding: Shows a lead circulating a one-page brief, giving each group equal time and recording the decision with reasons.

subtype: Approach: holding a structured decision meeting [Action]
passage:
'Everyone has the one-page brief?' Jyoti asked. Eight heads nodded. 'Three options for the warehouse system: fix the old one, buy the vendor product, or build our own. Costs and risks are on the page. Each team gets five minutes. Maria, operations first.'
Maria stood. 'Building our own takes eighteen months. We can't wait that long; our pickers are losing an hour a day now.'
'Noted. Finance?'
'The vendor option is cheapest over five years, if the licence price holds.'
'IT?'
'The vendor product doesn't talk to our billing system without extra work.'
After forty minutes, Jyoti wrote on the board: 'Decision: vendor product, with a budget for billing integration. Reasons: fastest relief for operations, lowest five-year cost.' She read it aloud. 'This goes in the minutes today. Anyone who disagrees, tell me why by Friday.'
Maria sat back. 'At least we all got heard.'

qa.q: How long would building their own system take?
How does Maria seem to feel at the end?
qa.a: Maria seems satisfied, even relieved, that every team got heard, whatever the outcome.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti do to make the decision stick?
qa.a: She could share the minutes with the reasons, answer any Friday objections openly and review the choice after the first few months.

qa.q: How might the IT team see the decision?
qa.a: IT's concern about billing was heard and given a budget, so they may accept the choice even though it adds work.

grounding: It shows a lead circulating a one-page brief of options, costs and risks, giving each group five minutes and recording the decision and reasons.

subtype: Approach: holding a structured decision meeting [Action]
passage:
I'm Trisha, and last month I ran my first decision meeting that didn't end in shouting. We had to choose a city for the new support centre: Jaipur, Kochi or Indore. Before, these meetings were a free-for-all. This time I sent a one-page brief two days early: three options, costs, hiring risks, travel time. In the meeting, each department got exactly five minutes, timer on the table. I said nothing except 'thank you, next'.
Nilesh from HR argued hard for Kochi. When the group chose Indore, I wrote the reasons on the board: lower rents, faster hiring, one direct flight. I emailed the notes within an hour.
Nilesh stopped me in the corridor later. 'I still think Kochi was better,' he said. 'But I get why. It felt fair.' That was the part I wanted.

qa.q: How long did each department get to speak?
qa.a: Exactly five minutes, with a timer on the table.

qa.q: How does Trisha feel about Nilesh's comment in the corridor?
qa.a: Trisha feels satisfied and proud, because fairness was exactly what the meeting was meant to achieve.

qa.q: What else could Trisha add to make future decisions even fairer?
qa.a: Trisha could invite written comments after the notes go out and state when the decision will be reviewed.

qa.q: How did the meeting look to Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh still preferred Kochi, but seeing the reasons written down after everyone was heard made the process feel fair to him.

grounding: It shows a lead sending a one-page brief with options, costs and risks, giving each group five minutes and recording the decision and reasons.
